Index lookups match by type, so mixed types silently split results.
  • Stock lives in inventory { _id: sku, product_id, available, reserved, updated_at }, updated by the order and warehouse services; the product document carries only a coarse in_stock flag (or per-variant flags) updated on transitions (in stock ↔ out of stock), not on every unit. Checkout reads inventory, never the product document.
  • Reviews and questions in their own collections keyed by product_id and time (index {product_id: 1, created_at: -1}), with the subset pattern: the newest five and the rating summary maintained on the product by an asynchronous worker.
  • Price. The price shown comes from the variant; checkout re-reads the price by SKU (and a price version) and refuses a stale cart line rather than silently charging differently.
  • Price history and analytics. A change stream on products/variants (with full documents or pre-images where needed) written into the warehouse as SCD2 price rows per SKU; the operational document never accumulates history.
  • Indexes. _id (product page); {category_path: 1, "attrs.k": 1, "attrs.v": 1} or the attribute index plus category; { "variants.size": 1, "variants.price.amount_minor": 1 } for variant filters — but not combined with attrs in one compound index when both are arrays; the missing-attribute report runs in the warehouse or with {category_path:1} plus $not: {$elemMatch: {k: "X"}} at low priority.

Competing designs to accept. Variants always in their own collection with a summary on the product (more writes, simpler size control). Wildcard index on an attributes sub-document instead of the k/v pattern, with its limits stated. A separate search engine for faceted listings fed by change streams, with the document database as the system of record. Bucketing reviews into documents of N reviews each.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Unbounded embedded arrays (reviews, price history) growing towards the size limit and making every write rewrite a large document; parallel-array compound indexes; attribute values of mixed types splitting index matches; stock embedded in a hot document; $lookup on the hottest page; analysts scanning the operational cluster.

Incident guidance.

  • Product with {{max_variants}} variants fails on the size limit and the import retries forever: quarantine the failing document so the feed continues (a dead-letter collection with the error), and stop retrying a non-retryable error. Fix the model: move variants out above the cut-over with a summary on the product. Guardrail: a size estimate check in the import (reject or route large products before insert) and an alert on documents above a fraction of the limit.
  • Compound index on two array fields fails to build: the index cannot be built because some documents have both fields as arrays. Contain by shipping the feature on an index that has one array field plus a post-filter, or restructure (per-variant documents, or tags moved into attrs). Guardrail: an index plan reviewed against the schema (which fields are arrays) before the release that depends on it, and index builds run in staging on a production-shaped copy.
  • Hot product document updated hundreds of times a second for stock: move stock to inventory keyed by SKU; update the product's in-stock flag only on transitions; cache product pages for seconds. Guardrail: a design rule that counters with high write rates never live in documents with high read rates, and monitoring of write conflicts per collection.

Follow-up guidance. (1) e.g. {{max_variants}} × ~0.5 KB plus translations; state the cut-over and that the page then reads product + variants by product_id (two reads, both indexed) or a summary only. (2) { attrs: {$elemMatch: {k: "waterproof", v: true}}, variants: {$elemMatch: {size: 44, "price.amount_minor": {$lt: 12000}}} }; one multikey index can serve one of the two conditions; the strongest answers note which and why. (3) Stock in inventory; the listing filters on the coarse flag and the product page reads exact stock by SKU. (4) A background job in batches with an updateMany per range, writing both keys during the transition and the reader accepting both, then removing the old key. (5) History downstream from a change stream (SCD2 in the warehouse); the operational document stays small.

Rubric anchors. 2: everything embedded including reviews and stock, no index for attribute filters, or a column per attribute. 3: bounded embedding with a size estimate, attribute pattern with one compound index, reviews and stock separated, a validator. 4: also the parallel-array constraint, a variant cut-over with a summary, type discipline through an attribute dictionary, price consistency with checkout and history through change streams.

Strong signals. Starts from access patterns and sizes before drawing documents; names the multikey limitation unprompted. Red flags. "Documents are schemaless, so no validation"; embedding unbounded arrays; one collection per category.

MDB-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Write rate. {{devices}} devices every {{interval}}: at 1 million devices every 10 seconds that is 100,000 readings a second; the candidate should do this arithmetic for the instance's values and size the cluster (and decide on sharding) from it.
  • Collection. readings as a time-series collection: timeField: "ts", metaField: "meta" with meta: {device_id, model} only. Site and firmware are not in the metaField: they change, and a change would start new buckets and split one device's series; they live in a devices dimension (with history) and are joined in rollups by validity interval. Measurements (temp, vib, power) are top-level fields.
  • Granularity. Chosen from the interval: seconds for 1-second readings, minutes for 1-minute readings (or custom bucketMaxSpanSeconds / bucketRoundingSeconds for the exact span). Readings per bucket = bucket span ÷ interval, capped by the bucket's count and size limits; the candidate should state an estimate and why a bucket of 1 reading or of a whole day is bad (compression and index size versus bucket size limits).
  • Indexes. The time-series collection's default/created index on { "meta.device_id": 1, ts: -1 } (per-device dashboard); a secondary on { "meta.model": 1, ts: 1 } if model queries are common.
  • Latest reading. device_latest { _id: device_id, ts, values }, updated by the ingest service with a conditional update (only if the new ts is newer), so late readings never overwrite a newer value.
  • Rollups. readings_hourly and readings_daily (regular collections or time-series collections with coarser granularity), keyed by (device_id, hour), computed by an aggregation with $merge (replace on key), so re-running an hour is idempotent. Late readings: the ingest records the touched (device, hour) in a dirty_hours collection; a recompute job re-aggregates those hours and their days. Site-level rollups join devices by validity interval of the site assignment.
  • Retention. expireAfterSeconds = {{retention_days}} days on raw; hourly for 2 years, daily indefinitely (or archived to object storage); a reading that arrives older than the raw retention is dropped and counted, but (if desired) still applied to rollups before being dropped.
  • Bad clocks. Readings with ts far in the past or future (before device activation, or more than a tolerance ahead) go to a quarantine collection with the arrival time; a device that reboots with an epoch clock is corrected using the device's monotonic counter if available, otherwise kept in quarantine.
  • Sharding. If the write rate needs it, shard on meta.device_id (hashed or ranged by a device prefix) so per-device queries are targeted; site-wide queries scatter but run against rollups.

Competing designs to accept. Ordinary collections with a manual bucket pattern (one document per device per hour with an array of readings), if they explain why time-series collections do this for them and what they would lose. Rollups in the warehouse instead of the operational cluster, if the dashboard's freshness is met. Firmware in the metaField if they show what happens at a firmware change and accept it.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. High-cardinality values in the metaField (a bucket per reading); granularity too coarse or too fine for the interval; late readings landing in rollups that are never recomputed; TTL expiring buckets that late data was still extending; bad clocks writing readings that expire on arrival; "latest" overwritten by a late reading; queries by site scanning raw data.

Incident guidance.

  • Per-reading message id copied into the metaField: contain by fixing the ingest mapping (meta is a fixed allowlist of fields) and, for the affected window, re-insert the readings into a corrected collection (or let the bad buckets expire if the window is short and the data is duplicated elsewhere). Guardrail: a schema contract on meta at ingest, and an alert on buckets per device per hour above the expected value.
  • Six days of buffered readings from one site: accept them (they are within retention); mark the touched hours dirty and recompute hourly and daily rollups for that site; suppress alerts computed on readings older than the alert's own window, or evaluate alerts only on readings near real time. With {{late_share}} late on a normal day, the recompute must be routine, not exceptional. Guardrail: alerts keyed on arrival lag, and a rollup "last recomputed" timestamp shown on dashboards.
  • 1970 clocks expired immediately with a calibration record: quarantine readings with impossible timestamps before they reach the TTL collection; keep calibration records in their own regular collection, never in an expiring one. Guardrail: a lower bound on accepted timestamps (device activation date) and a counter of quarantined readings per firmware version.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Arithmetic from the instance; readings per bucket = span ÷ interval for one device. (2) Goes to (or creates) a bucket for that device and time; it costs an extra bucket write and may reduce compression; recompute the dirty hour and day. (3) Define "per site" as the site the device was in at reading time (join on the assignment's validity interval); recompute last month after the history is right. (4) Recompute rollups from dirty hours before raw data is deleted, with a margin; or apply late readings to rollups at ingest. (5) Shard on device id if writes need it; per-device queries targeted, site queries served by rollups.

Rubric anchors. 2: one document per reading in a regular collection, or everything (including site and firmware) in the metaField, no plan for late data. 3: correct metaField and granularity with an estimate, latest-reading collection, rollups with $merge, TTL retention. 4: also dirty-hour recomputation, time-varying device attributes handled by validity interval, bucket-level expiry semantics, bad-clock quarantine and a targeted shard key.

Strong signals. Computes the write rate and readings per bucket before naming settings. Red flags. Sequence numbers or request ids in the metaField; rollups computed once and never corrected; "late data is rare, ignore it".

MDB-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Criteria first. Cardinality (enough distinct values to split), frequency (no value that holds a large share), monotonicity (no "always the newest chunk"), and query targeting (the main queries carry the key's prefix).
  • Candidates for activity.
    • {tenant_id: 1}: targeted by tenant, but the largest tenant ({{largest_tenant_share}} of the data) is one key value: its chunk cannot be split (jumbo), cannot be moved, and fills one shard.
    • {tenant_id: 1, _id: 1} with time-ordered ids: splittable, targeted; but each tenant's inserts go to the last chunk of its range, so the largest tenant's writes hit one shard (a hot chunk).
    • {tenant_id: 1, project_id: 1, _id: 1}: targeted for "latest activity in a project" (index scan in order); inserts for a large tenant spread across its projects' chunks, if projects are many and similar in size.
    • {tenant_id: 1, _id: "hashed"}: tenant-targeted, inserts for a tenant spread over its range; "latest in project" becomes a tenant-targeted query with a secondary index {tenant_id, project_id, _id: -1} on each shard holding the tenant.
    • {_id: "hashed"}: perfect spread, but every query without _id is scatter-gather, and residency zones become impossible because ranges no longer map to tenants.
    • Recommended: {tenant_id, project_id, _id} or {tenant_id, hashed _id}, with the trade-off stated.
  • Small collections. users and projects may stay unsharded (or sharded on tenant_id) if they fit; sharding them adds routing cost without benefit.
  • Residency. Prefix ranges per residency tenant: zone eu covers [{tenant_id: T, …: MinKey}, {tenant_id: T, …: MaxKey}) for each EU tenant, or tenant ids allocated from region-specific ranges so one zone range covers a region. Non-residency tenants unconstrained.
  • Region change. Plan: add the new zone range for the tenant (the old one removed in the same change), let the balancer move the chunks, monitor progress; the application keeps working because routing follows chunk ownership; the residency rule is met only when every chunk has moved, so the move starts early enough to finish before the deadline, off-peak, with migration throttling. For contractual strictness, copy-then-switch to a new tenant id range is an alternative.
  • Email lookup. A small user_directory {email, tenant_id, user_id} collection (unsharded or sharded on email), then a targeted query.
  • Monitoring. Data size and chunk count per shard, jumbo chunk count, share of queries that are scatter-gather, insert rate per shard, top tenants by data size and growth; thresholds for action: refine the key (add a suffix), reshard, or move a whale tenant to a dedicated cluster with application routing.

Competing designs to accept. Dedicated clusters for the largest tenants and a shared sharded cluster for the long tail. One collection per tenant (only for small tenant counts; at {{tenants}} it strains metadata). A region-first key {region, tenant_id, …} for residency, if they handle region changes as key changes (which are document rewrites).

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Jumbo chunks for large tenants, hot last chunks with monotonic suffixes, scatter-gather from hashed _id, zones defined on fields that are not a key prefix, region moves started too late or at peak, metadata growth from per-tenant collections.

Incident guidance.

  • Jumbo chunks for the largest tenant fill one shard: contain by adding disk or moving other chunks off that shard; plan a key change: refine the shard key with a suffix so chunks can split, or reshard to a compound key, or move the tenant to a dedicated cluster. Guardrail: alert on jumbo chunks and on any single key value above a share of a shard's data.
  • Hot last chunk for the largest tenant: a monotonic suffix within a tenant concentrates inserts. Switch to a hashed suffix or a project-based middle field (refine or reshard); short-term, pre-split and distribute that tenant's future range. Guardrail: per-shard insert rate in the dashboard, and a load test of the key with a production-shaped tenant distribution.
  • Region change during peak, documents in two regions: pause the balancer for that collection outside a window or throttle migrations; schedule zone changes off-peak with a runbook; for strict residency, track the move as incomplete until every chunk is on the target zone, and inform the tenant of the window. Guardrail: zone changes only through a change process with a migration-time estimate, and a residency check that lists any chunk of a residency tenant outside its zone.

Follow-up guidance. (1) One key value: unsplittable, unmovable, one shard. (2) Project-prefixed key gives ordered reads per project; hashed suffix spreads inserts but needs a secondary index for ordered reads. (3) The zone runbook above. (4) A directory collection. (5) Signals: jumbo chunks, per-shard size skew, per-shard insert rate, scatter-gather share; decide by thresholds.

Rubric anchors. 2: picks hashed _id or tenant_id alone without seeing the consequences. 3: compares candidates on the four criteria, picks a compound tenant-prefixed key, explains jumbo and hot chunks, defines zones as key ranges. 4: also region-change runbook with residency during moves, email lookup without scatter-gather, monitoring with thresholds, and a reasoned choice between refine, reshard and dedicated clusters.

Strong signals. States the key criteria before candidates; asks for the tenant size distribution. Red flags. "Hashed keys solve everything"; ignoring residency during migrations; sharding every collection.

MDB-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Version field. schema_version (int) on every document, indexed. Step 0: a one-off classification job (shape detection) stamps a version on unversioned documents, with a report of documents it could not classify; after that, the version field is the only truth.
  • Application. A reader per version that maps to the current in-memory model; writes always in the newest version (upgrade on write). Releases are forward compatible: the release before a new shape learns to read it and to preserve unknown fields (no full-document replace from a model that drops fields), so rolling back never loses data. Expand → migrate → contract: add the new field and read both, then backfill, then stop writing/reading the old field.
  • Backfill. Iterate by _id range in batches (for example 500–1,000 documents) over {schema_version: {$lt: N}}, each document upgraded with a conditional update: updateOne({_id, schema_version: v, updated_at: t}, {$set: {...new}, $unset: {...old}, $set: {schema_version: N}}); if it matches nothing, a concurrent writer won: re-read and retry. Checkpoint the last _id processed for resumption. Throttle on replication lag (pause when lag on any secondary passes a budget well inside the oplog window), on primary write latency and on oplog churn per hour versus oplog size. Write concern majority per batch so the backfill cannot outrun replication.
  • Completion proof. Count per schema_version (from the index) reaching zero for old versions; then tighten the $jsonSchema validator to the newest version and remove old readers.
  • Warehouse. Change stream with fullDocument: "updateLookup" (or pre/post images where available), or periodic snapshots plus change events. A staging layer maps each version explicitly to one model: v1 dollars (decimal) → cents (round(amount*100)), v2 cents; v1 single address → list with one entry of type "primary"; unknown versions go to a quarantine table and fail the load. A reconciliation compares revenue totals by day across versions against the billing system.

Competing designs to accept. Migrate on read only (lazy), with a final backfill for the untouched tail. A copy-and-swap migration into a new collection with dual writes and a cut-over, if they handle reads during it and the cost at {{documents}}. A view per version in the warehouse instead of a staging model, if unknown versions still fail loudly.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Shape detection used forever instead of a version field; unthrottled backfill causing lag and an oplog that rolls past a secondary; backfill overwriting concurrent updates; rollbacks that drop unknown fields; warehouse mapping keyed on a field both versions share; no proof that old versions are gone.

Incident guidance.

  • Unthrottled backfill, secondary fell off the oplog: stop the backfill; resync the stale secondary (initial sync) and keep the set's write concern achievable meanwhile; resume the backfill with throttling on replication lag and a batch size that keeps oplog churn well inside the window, possibly with a temporarily larger oplog. Guardrail: the backfill tool refuses to run without a lag budget and pauses automatically; alert on lag approaching the oplog window.
  • Revenue 100 times too high after cents: the mapping chose by a field both versions have, so cents were multiplied again. Fix the mapping to switch on schema_version; recompute affected days; reconcile with billing before publishing. With {{versions_live}} versions live, a test per version with a known document is required. Guardrail: daily reconciliation of revenue against the billing system, and load failure on unknown or ambiguous versions.
  • Rollback dropped new address fields: restore the lost fields from the change stream history or backups for the affected documents; fix the old release to preserve unknown fields (partial $set updates instead of replacing the document). Guardrail: the expand-then-contract rule and a rollback test that runs the previous release against documents in the new shape before any release that changes the shape.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Untouched after D days ≈ (1 − {{daily_touched}})^D for uniform touches (real touches are skewed: many accounts are never written), so the backfill covers most documents at low touch rates. (2) Conditional update on version and updated_at; the plan change wins, the backfill retries on the new state. (3) Throttle on lag and latency; checkpoint by _id; prove by counts per version. (4) Forward-compatible release; partial updates preserve fields; the rollback is safe because the previous release already understood the shape. (5) Mapping keyed on version; reconciliation catches the jump.

Rubric anchors. 2: "just run an updateMany" or "the application handles all versions forever". 3: explicit version, upgrade on write plus a throttled resumable backfill, versioned warehouse mapping. 4: also conditional updates against concurrent writers, oplog-window reasoning, forward-compatible releases for rollback, completion proof and reconciliation.

Strong signals. Separates the read path, the write path and the backfill; asks how big the oplog is. Red flags. A single updateMany over billions of documents; full-document replace from a model that does not know new fields; analytics that guess versions.

MDB-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{ns_raw}}, {{window_start}}, {{window_end}}, {{t1}}, {{t2}}, {{t3}}, {{tier_a}} and {{tier_b}} come from the instance; at Medium the three thresholds are equal and the tiers are 0)

WITH ev AS (
  SELECT * FROM chunk_events WHERE ns = '{{ns_raw}}'
), hours AS (
  SELECT h AS hour_start, h + INTERVAL '1 hour' AS hour_end
  FROM generate_series(TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_start}}',
                       TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_end}}' - INTERVAL '1 hour',
                       INTERVAL '1 hour') AS g(h)
), born AS (                                   -- one row per chunk, however many rows created it
  SELECT chunk_id, MIN(occurred_at) AS born_at
  FROM ev
  WHERE kind IN ('create', 'split', 'merge')
  GROUP BY chunk_id
), retired AS (
  SELECT source_chunk_id AS chunk_id, MIN(occurred_at) AS retired_at
  FROM ev
  WHERE kind IN ('split', 'merge')
  GROUP BY source_chunk_id
), owner_change AS (                           -- move_start and move_abort never change the owner
  SELECT chunk_id, shard_id, occurred_at, event_id
  FROM ev
  WHERE kind IN ('create', 'split', 'merge', 'move_commit')
), layout AS (
  SELECT h.hour_start, b.chunk_id,
         (SELECT o.shard_id
            FROM owner_change o
           WHERE o.chunk_id = b.chunk_id AND o.occurred_at < h.hour_end
           ORDER BY o.occurred_at DESC, o.event_id DESC
           LIMIT 1) AS shard_id
  FROM hours h
  JOIN born b ON b.born_at < h.hour_end
  LEFT JOIN retired x ON x.chunk_id = b.chunk_id
  WHERE x.retired_at IS NULL OR x.retired_at >= h.hour_end
), per_shard AS (                              -- every active shard, empty ones with 0
  SELECT h.hour_start, s.shard_id, COUNT(l.chunk_id) AS chunks
  FROM hours h
  JOIN shards s ON s.added_at < h.hour_end
  LEFT JOIN layout l ON l.hour_start = h.hour_start AND l.shard_id = s.shard_id
  GROUP BY h.hour_start, s.shard_id
), per_hour AS (
  SELECT hour_start, COUNT(*) AS active_shards, SUM(chunks) AS total_chunks,
         MAX(chunks) AS max_chunks, MIN(chunks) AS min_chunks
  FROM per_shard
  GROUP BY hour_start
), top_shard AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (hour_start) hour_start, shard_id
  FROM per_shard
  ORDER BY hour_start, chunks DESC, shard_id
)
SELECT p.hour_start, p.active_shards, p.total_chunks, p.max_chunks, p.min_chunks,
       p.max_chunks - p.min_chunks AS imbalance,
       t.shard_id AS most_loaded_shard,
       p.max_chunks - p.min_chunks >= CASE WHEN p.total_chunks < {{tier_a}} THEN {{t1}}
                                           WHEN p.total_chunks < {{tier_b}} THEN {{t2}}
                                           ELSE {{t3}} END AS needs_balancing
FROM per_hour p
JOIN top_shard t USING (hour_start)
ORDER BY p.hour_start;

Explanation. The report is a state reconstruction, not an aggregation of events: each hour needs the whole layout as it stood at the end of the hour, so the hours are generated first and quiet hours carry the layout forward. A chunk exists from its first creating row (create, split child, merge result) until the first row that names it as a source; its owner as of a time is the latest ownership row before that time, where only committed migrations move a chunk. Because a split row already carries the owning shard, nothing has to be inherited recursively. Counts start from the active shards (added strictly before the hour's end) and LEFT JOIN the layout, so an empty shard counts as 0; one DISTINCT ON row per hour applies the tie rule. Every boundary is strict: an event or shard addition at exactly hh:00:00 belongs to the hour that starts then.

Complexity. The correlated owner lookup runs once per (hour, live chunk) with an index on (chunk_id, occurred_at); the cross product of hours and chunks is small here. At production scale, compute ownership intervals once — LEAD(occurred_at) OVER (PARTITION BY chunk_id ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id) over ownership rows, clipped by the retirement time — and join hours to intervals with start < hour_end AND (end IS NULL OR end >= hour_end); or keep a daily snapshot of the layout and replay only the day's events.

Dialect notes. generate_series over timestamps and DISTINCT ON are PostgreSQL. Snowflake builds hours with GENERATOR / ROW_NUMBER() and DATEADD, BigQuery with GENERATE_TIMESTAMP_ARRAY and UNNEST, Spark SQL with sequence(start, stop, INTERVAL 1 HOUR) and explode. The tie rule becomes QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY hour_start ORDER BY chunks DESC, shard_id) = 1 (Snowflake, BigQuery) or a row-number subquery (Spark, MySQL 8). Correlated ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 subqueries are not supported in every engine (BigQuery and Spark restrict them); use the LEAD interval form there. MySQL 8 has no generate_series: a recursive CTE builds the hours. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. A shard that is active but empty for the first hours (Medium: added before the window; Hard: added during it; Very Hard: added exactly on an hour boundary); a migration committed exactly on an hour boundary; an hour with no events at all; events after the window end; chunks split several times in a chain. Hard adds move_start and move_abort rows (including at least one abandoned migration in the window, whose destination never owns the chunk) and a second collection in the export. Very Hard adds merges (two or three rows for one new chunk, every source retired) and three-way splits. Ties for the most loaded shard occur often.

Common mistakes. Grouping events by date_trunc('hour', occurred_at) (counts changes, not the layout, and drops quiet hours); <= at the hour end; keeping split parents alive; an inner join that drops empty shards; (Hard+) taking the latest migration row of any kind as the owner, forgetting the ns filter, counting a shard before it was added; (Very Hard) counting merge rows instead of distinct chunks, or not retiring merge sources. Each has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Ownership intervals with LEAD, retirement as an interval end, an interval join to hours; or daily snapshots plus replay. (2) Export a snapshot of the current chunk metadata (each chunk with its owner) on a schedule and replay only changelog rows after the snapshot; alert when the oldest changelog row is newer than the last snapshot. (3) Needs data size per chunk (from split and migration details, or periodic size statistics); a shard with few chunks can hold a jumbo chunk, so counts and sizes disagree. (4) Rank chunks per shard on the most loaded shards and take the excess over (min + threshold − 1); a window function over the latest hour's layout.

Rubric anchors. 2: groups events by hour or drops quiet hours; split parents still counted. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains interval-based scaling, the capped-changelog baseline, and why chunk counts differ from data balance.

Strong signals. Says "this is a state as of a time" and generates the hours first; asks what changes an owner. Red flags. SELECT DISTINCT to fix double counts without knowing why; treating move_start as ownership; an inner join from chunks to shards.

       p.max_chunks - p.min_chunks >= CASE WHEN p.total_chunks < {{tier_a}} THEN {{t1}}
                                           WHEN p.total_chunks < {{tier_b}} THEN {{t2}}
                                           ELSE {{t3}} END AS needs_balancing
FROM per_hour p
JOIN top_shard t USING (hour_start)
ORDER BY p.hour_start;

MDB-L4-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Identity and topology: every sample carries member_id (stable for the life of a process host, new when a member is replaced), cluster_id, shard_id (or none), role, sample_ts, agent_seq. Topology is a separate event table (member_id, cluster_id, shard_id, valid_from, valid_to) fed by the control plane, so a chart for a cluster joins samples to the members it had at each moment. Members are never renamed in place.
  • Ingestion: agents batch samples per {{sample_seconds}}-second tick, compress, and send to a regional ingestion tier (authenticated per agent, which fixes the tenant). A durable log partitioned by cluster_id keeps a cluster's members together and ordered. Ingestion computes rates from cumulative counters per (member, counter): rate = (v − v_prev) / (t − t_prev), and when v < v_prev or the process start time changed, it treats the interval as a reset (rate from v / (t − process_start) or a gap), never a negative rate. Samples carry their own sample_ts; late samples are accepted into the right time bucket.
  • Storage: (a) a hot store with raw samples for a few days, keyed (tenant, cluster_id, metric, member_id, ts), sized for chart reads of one cluster; (b) rollups at 1 minute and 1 hour with sum, count, min, max for rates and gauges and a mergeable latency histogram or sketch for percentiles; (c) columnar history partitioned by day and tenant for fleet questions and retention to {{retention_days}} days (raw for days, minutes for weeks, hours beyond). A "latest value per series" table answers "largest replication lag right now" without a scan.
  • Alerting: a stream evaluator keyed by cluster holds per-rule state (condition true since, last sample time). It evaluates on event time with a small allowed lateness, so a condition held for the rule's duration fires within {{alert_minutes}} minutes. Missing data is its own state ("no data for N intervals"), never zero. Rules are indexed by (cluster, metric), so a sample only touches the rules that reference it.
  • Lag semantics: lag = primary's latest operation time − secondary's latest applied time, but on idle clusters the primary only advances every 10 seconds (this exercise's rule), so lag shows a 0–10 s sawtooth. Report lag as max(0, lag − idle_allowance) when the primary had no user writes in the interval, or report "time since the secondary last caught up", and document it.
  • Disk projection: a fit over several horizons (hours and days) with known transient consumers (index builds, compaction, initial syncs) annotated from control-plane events; alert on the long-horizon projection, warn on the short one.
  • Isolation and cost: every read API takes the tenant from the authenticated principal, not from the request; fleet views live behind a separate operator API. Per-tenant query quotas and cached chart tiles protect the store from export jobs. Cost per cluster stays flat because storage per series is fixed by retention and rollup policy, and series count scales with members, not with time.

Competing designs to accept. A general-purpose time-series database (with cardinality limits addressed) instead of a custom store; computing rates at query time if resets are detected there correctly; regional stores with a federated fleet view; pulling metrics from members instead of agent push, if the candidate covers scale and member churn.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Series cardinality explosion from labels (per-database or per-collection metrics); negative or giant rates after restarts; late or out-of-order batches mis-evaluated by wall-clock alerting; idle-primary lag artefacts; one tenant's export saturating the store; projection alerts that cry wolf.

Incident guidance.

  • Rolling upgrade negative spikes: rates computed across a counter reset. Recompute affected windows with reset detection (process start time in every sample), mark the restart on charts, and rebuild the fleet "busiest" table. Prevention: reset handling at ingestion plus a test that replays a restart.
  • Idle-cluster lag 0–10 s paging: the idle primary's 10-second no-op makes lag a sawtooth. Change the lag definition for idle intervals (or compare against the last no-op), suppress the page, and tell the customer what changed. Prevention: documented lag semantics and a synthetic idle-cluster test.
  • 40-minute regional backlog: wall-clock evaluation either dropped late samples or fired late. Evaluate on event time; for samples older than allowed lateness, evaluate retrospectively and send "condition held from … to …" notices rather than live pages; alert on agent connectivity separately. Prevention: per-region ingestion health and "no data" as a first-class state.
  • Index-build disk projections: short-horizon linear fit sees a transient. Annotate known transient operations, require the long-horizon projection to agree, and cap alert volume per run. Prevention: backtest projections against real disk-full events and track precision.

Follow-up guidance. Push on counter resets, the meaning of lag on an idle cluster, alert evaluation with late data, and cardinality at the top of {{clusters}}. A strong candidate quantifies: e.g. members × metrics × samples per day, and bytes per sample after compression.

Rubric anchors. 2: "send everything to a time-series database and alert on thresholds"; no resets, no late data, no isolation. 3: stable member identity, reset-aware rates, hot store plus rollups, stream alert evaluation with no-data states, tenant isolation. 4: also lag semantics for idle primaries, event-time alerting with retrospective notices, histogram rollups for percentiles, quotas, cost per cluster reasoning, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Asks what the metrics are used for before choosing stores; treats topology as history. Red flags. Treats missing samples as zero; computes percentiles by averaging per-minute percentiles; customer ids taken from the request body.

MDB-L4-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Plan: compute the new key's initial ranges from a sample of documents (so the new layout starts balanced), assign ranges to receiving shards, check free disk on each receiver against its share of {{collection_tb}} TB, and check every source shard's oplog window against the estimated copy time with margin. If the window is too short, enlarge the oplog first (it is the customer's cluster; say so in the plan) or add capacity to speed the copy.
  • Copy (clone): record a start cluster time T0. Each receiver reads from every source shard the documents whose new key falls into its ranges, as of T0 (a snapshot read), writes them into a temporary collection, then builds the collection's indexes. Throttle to keep ordinary p99 under twice normal.
  • Catch-up: each receiver tails every source shard's oplog from T0, filters entries for the collection, maps each changed document to its new owner and applies it idempotently (upserts and deletes by _id, replaying entries in order per source). Transactions are applied as units. Each receiver tracks its applied position per source; the coordinator tracks the estimated time to apply what remains.
  • Commit gate and switch: when the remaining lag is small enough to apply in less than {{block_seconds}} seconds at the measured rate (and the source rate is not at peak), the coordinator blocks writes to the collection on the sources, waits for receivers to apply up to the final position, verifies, then commits a single metadata change on the config servers (new layout, new collection version). Routers refresh and route by the new key; writes resume. If the gate is not met within a time budget, wait or defer to a quieter window; never start the block hoping to catch up.
  • Retried writes and transactions: the retry history (session id and transaction number → result) of writes that touched the collection is copied to the new owners during catch-up and at commit, so a retried write after the switch is recognised and not applied twice. Transactions in progress at the block are aborted and retried by the driver.
  • Verification: at a chosen cluster time (the commit point), per-range document counts and order-independent hashes of documents (e.g. sum of hashes) computed on old and new layouts and compared; sampled full-document comparison during catch-up. After commit, old copies are deleted in the background, and reports filter documents a shard does not own until cleanup finishes.
  • Abort: before commit, aborting drops the temporary collections on receivers and stops catch-up; the old layout was never modified. After commit there is no automatic rollback; a reverse reshard is a new operation.
  • Change streams: the collection's change stream continues across the commit with a resharding event; tokens from before the switch remain resumable as long as the oplog covers them (this exercise's rule; check current docs). Consumers should tolerate the event.
  • Customer view: estimated duration, disk and cost impact, progress, the gate status, a scheduled or approved switch, and the ability to abort.

Competing designs to accept. Application-level dual writes with a backfill and read switch (more control, more application work, harder transactions); copying into a new collection and renaming at the end; adding temporary shards to speed the copy; a chunk-by-chunk migration if the candidate shows how the key change is achieved.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Oplog window shorter than the copy; receivers that cannot keep up with peak writes; disk exhaustion on receivers; long index builds after the copy; retried writes and in-flight transactions at the switch; unique constraints that are only enforced per shard; leftover old copies counted by reports.

Incident guidance.

  • Oplog overwritten at catch-up: the operation cannot continue safely; abort and clean up. Next attempt: enlarge the source oplogs (or the window via retention settings) to cover the copy with margin, raise the copy rate during quiet hours, and monitor "time until the oldest needed entry is overwritten" as a first-class gauge that pauses or aborts early.
  • Cannot catch up at peak: do not start the block. Defer the switch to a low-traffic window, temporarily raise receiver apply parallelism, and alert the customer with the estimate. Prevention: the gate is computed from measured rates, and the plan schedules the switch window up front.
  • Increment applied twice after retry: retry history (session id and transaction number) was not carried to the new owner, so it could not recognise the retry. Find affected writes by matching session and transaction numbers in the old and new owners' oplogs, correct the counts with the customer, and carry retry history at commit. Also note for the candidate: non-idempotent updates ($inc) depend on that history, while a unique index can only be enforced across shards when it is prefixed by the shard key (this exercise's rule; check current docs).
  • 0.03% more documents in reports: the report counted leftover documents on shards that no longer own them. Make reports and counts ownership-aware (filter by the routing table) and track cleanup progress; prevention: a post-commit cleanup monitor and a documented "orphan" state.

Follow-up guidance. Push on the oplog window arithmetic, the commit gate, and retried writes across the switch. Strong candidates estimate copy time from {{collection_tb}} TB and a throttled rate, and compare it with the window.

Rubric anchors. 2: "copy the data to a new collection and switch the application"; no catch-up or a long write outage. 3: snapshot copy at a cluster time, oplog catch-up with idempotent application, a bounded switch, verification by counts, abort before commit. 4: also oplog-window planning, a measured commit gate, retry history and transactions across the switch, hash verification at one cluster time, ownership-aware cleanup, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Starts with the arithmetic (size, rate, window); separates reversible from irreversible steps. Red flags. Long write outages; no plan for changes during the copy; "verify by counting rows" on a moving collection with no fixed time.

MDB-L4-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Placement: with three serving regions, five members as 2-2-1 (the region with one member holds a lower priority), or 2-2-1 with the single member in a third, non-serving site; losing any region leaves at least three of five votes. With two serving regions on one continent, two data-bearing members per region plus a fifth voting member in a third site (a data-bearing member preferred over an arbiter), since without a third site the loss of the region holding the majority stops writes. With two continents and two regions each, five or seven members spread so no single region holds a majority (for example 2-2-2-1 with seven voting members), priorities favouring the continent where most writes originate.
  • Priorities and roles: highest priority on members in the primary's preferred region, next in the nearest other region, zero priority for a member in a far or tie-breaker site so it never becomes primary; hidden members (priority 0, no reads) for analytics or backup; a delayed member only as protection against bad writes, never counted on for majority writes.
  • Write concern: orders w: majority (with journaling), so an acknowledged order survives any single-region loss; activity feed may use acknowledgement by the primary only if the loss rule allows it. Cost: a majority write waits for the nearest secondary that completes the majority, roughly one inter-region round trip if a majority is not within the primary's region.
  • Reads: "my orders" after placing an order: read from the primary, or a causally consistent session whose operation time is carried by the application (in a cookie or token) so any server in any region reads at least that point with majority read concern; feed browsing reads nearest with a staleness bound.
  • Failure walk-through: primary region lost: after about 10 seconds an election (this exercise's rule) elects the highest-priority reachable member; drivers see errors on in-flight writes, retry once (retryable writes), rediscover the new primary; majority-acknowledged writes are all present. Partition: the cut-off primary cannot see a majority and steps down; the other side elects a primary; the cut-off region's application servers cannot write (they can only reach the old region's members) and may read stale data from local secondaries; route those customers to another region.

Competing designs to accept. Seven voting members for finer placement; an arbiter in the tie-breaker site if the candidate knows its cost with majority writes; region-local writes through sharding by region (zones) as a later step; accepting a manual failover for two-region setups if the candidate states it violates the constraint and proposes a third site.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Majority unavailable after losing the majority region; arbiter layouts that stall majority writes when a data-bearing member is down; w:1 rollbacks; stale reads from lagging secondaries; failover to a far region moving write latency; failback churn when a high-priority member returns.

Incident guidance.

  • Default write concern lowered, 4 s rolled back: the change violated {{loss_rule}}. Recover the rolled-back writes from the rollback files on the old primary and reconcile them against later writes (customers may have retried); restore w: majority for orders, and add a guard that rejects weaker defaults for the order collections. Prevention: write concern per collection or operation in code reviews and a test that kills the primary under load.
  • Arbiter layout, secondary down: with one data-bearing secondary down, majority writes cannot be satisfied; the primary keeps more history in its cache because the majority commit point does not advance. Bring the secondary back or temporarily reconfigure, lower write concern only where allowed, and replace the arbiter with a data-bearing member. Prevention: no arbiter where majority writes are required.
  • Region cut off 12 minutes: the old primary stepped down correctly; customers in that region saw frozen data. Route their traffic to healthy regions via the global load balancer, show a degraded notice, and ensure reads that need freshness go to the primary. Prevention: health checks that consider the replica set's view, not only the local region.
  • Write latency after failover: the primary moved away from the application servers. Move write traffic or let the original region's member become primary again in a controlled step once it is caught up. Prevention: plan priorities with latency in mind and test failback.

Follow-up guidance. Make the candidate count votes after each regional loss and count round trips per write. Probe read-your-own-writes across application servers in different regions.

Rubric anchors. 2: "three members in three regions, failover is automatic" with no vote arithmetic, write concern or read semantics. 3: correct placement and vote counting, majority writes for orders, read preferences per read, correct election behaviour. 4: also causal consistency across servers, arbiter and hidden or delayed member trade-offs, partition behaviour with step-down, latency accounting in inter-region round trips, failback, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Starts from the loss rule and vote arithmetic. Red flags. Believes w:1 writes are durable across failover; puts a majority of votes in one region; reads from secondaries for read-your-own-writes with no session.

MDB-L4-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Hierarchy: the customer's key (in their key management service) wraps a per-cluster master key (or per-member keys); the storage engine's data keys are wrapped by that master key; data files are encrypted with data keys. Only the wrapped master key is stored with the cluster. The service calls decrypt to unwrap the master key at member start; plaintext keys live only in member memory.
  • Access: the customer grants a role or principal used only by the service's key-access component, scoped to encrypt/decrypt on that key. A periodic health check (for example every few minutes) and the customer's own key events (permission or state change notifications where available) feed a key-access state per cluster.
  • Member start and replacement: a new or replaced member fetches the wrapped master key, calls decrypt with the customer's key, and starts. If the call fails it stays down and the cluster's status shows "key access failed" with the exact error returned.
  • Rotation: the customer rotates; the service detects the new primary key version and rewraps the master key with it (a decrypt + encrypt call), on every member, in every region, without restarting or rewriting data. Re-encrypting data files with new data keys is a separate, scheduled operation (rolling initial sync or file rewrite), offered for customers whose policy requires it.
  • Backups: each snapshot stores its data in encrypted form plus the wrapped key it needs, with a record of the customer key version used. A restore unwraps with that version. Before a customer deletes a key version, they can see (in the console and via API) which retained backups depend on it; the service warns at rotation time and fails restores with a precise message. Cross-region snapshot copies are wrapped by the destination region's key (or a linked multi-region key), recorded likewise.
  • Revocation: state machine healthy → access_failing → revoked (or outage). Distinguish permission/state errors (access denied, key disabled or scheduled for deletion) from availability errors (timeouts, 5xx, a regional outage of the key service). On confirmed revocation: block new member starts and restores, then perform an orderly shutdown of members within {{revoke_hours}} hours so in-memory keys are discarded, and stop backups. Recovery: once access returns, members start normally; deletion of the key is irreversible and makes data and backups unrecoverable, as the customer intended.
  • Audit: the key service's own logs in the customer's account record every decrypt/encrypt call by the service, with times; the service adds a per-cluster event log (rotation detected, rewrap done, access lost, shutdown done) the customer can export.

Competing designs to accept. Per-member master keys; client-side field-level encryption for the most sensitive fields in addition (the service then never sees those fields in plaintext); re-encrypting data at rotation if the candidate costs it; immediate shutdown at revocation if they handle outages separately.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Members unable to restart after a policy mistake; deleted key versions breaking old backups; replicas or copies in other regions using different keys; outages mistaken for revocation; exports outside the key's protection; throttling of key service calls when thousands of members restart at once.

Incident guidance.

  • Policy mistake, member stays down: the rolling patch must stop at the first member that cannot unwrap its key (a pre-check before restarting each member). Tell the customer the exact permission error; once fixed, the member starts. Prevention: pre-flight key access check before any planned restart, and alerting the customer when the periodic check starts failing.
  • Deleted key version, restore fails: the snapshot is wrapped by the deleted version; it cannot be restored. Say so plainly. Prevention: per-backup key-version dependency shown before deletion, a warning when a version with dependants is scheduled for deletion, and rewrapping retained backups to the new version at rotation (a cheap operation on the wrapped key) where the policy allows.
  • Revocation, second region still serving, unencrypted export: the second region's members held unwrapped keys and were not covered by the shutdown sequence, or used a linked key not revoked. Extend revocation to every member and copy wrapped by any version of the customer's key, and tell the customer exactly what remains (the export). Prevention: an inventory of every artefact per key and exports encrypted with the customer's key.
  • KMS outage treated as revocation: halt the automation, restart any stopped members once the key service returns, and post an incident note. Prevention: classify errors, require sustained permission errors before acting, and cap automated shutdowns per window with a human approval above the cap.

Follow-up guidance. Push on the difference between rewrapping and re-encrypting, on which key versions old backups need, and on how revocation reaches a member that never restarts.

Rubric anchors. 2: "encrypt the disk with the customer's key", no hierarchy, no backup or revocation story. 3: envelope hierarchy, start-time unwrap, rotation by rewrap, backups with key-version records, revocation detection and shutdown. 4: also outage versus revocation, bounded in-memory key lifetime, cross-region copies and exports, dependency warnings before deletion, auditable evidence from the key service, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Asks what "unreadable" must mean and for which artefacts. Red flags. Storing the customer's key in plaintext; claiming rotation re-encrypts data for free; no thought for old backups after rotation.

MDB-L4-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Snapshots: per shard (and config servers), a consistent snapshot from a secondary using a storage-level snapshot of a checkpoint-consistent data directory, or a database backup cursor; each records its shard and the cluster time it represents. Incremental snapshots copy only changed blocks after a full base; chains are bounded (a new full base periodically). Snapshots are taken from secondaries and throttled to keep load within a few percent.
  • Oplog capture: a capture process per shard tails the oplog from a secondary and writes slices to object storage, each slice (shard, first_ts, last_ts, checksum). Continuity rule: each slice starts right after the previous slice's last entry; any break is a recorded gap. A gauge per shard tracks "headroom" = time between the oldest entry still on the shard and the capture position; alerts at low headroom, and capture is never throttled below the shard's write rate. Captured oplog is kept for {{window}}.
  • Restore point: the customer picks a second; the system converts it to a cluster time (all entries with seconds ≤ chosen second, inclusive, defined in the console). For each shard: choose the latest snapshot at or before the point, restore it to new storage, start a member in a restore mode, and apply captured oplog entries in order up to the cluster time. A cross-shard transaction commits at one cluster time on all its shards, so stopping every shard at the same cluster time keeps it whole. Config server metadata is restored to the same point.
  • Time budget: restore time ≈ (bytes to copy / restore throughput) + (oplog hours since snapshot × {{oplog_gb_hour}} GB / replay throughput) + index and validation checks. Snapshots every {{snapshot_hours}} hours bound the replay; for tight {{rto_hours}} hours, keep more frequent incrementals or a continuously applied standby copy for premium tiers. The console shows an estimate before starting.
  • Verification: the restored cluster starts and passes collection and index validation; per-collection counts and hashes at the restore point compared with values recorded at snapshot time and adjusted by the replayed oplog (counts derived from oplog inserts and deletes); restored cluster time equals the requested point on every shard. Continuous drills: automatically restore a sample of clusters every day, verify, and record restore duration against the promise.
  • Retention: snapshots carry a policy class (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly) and expire by policy; deletion is reference-counted (active restores, incremental chains, legal holds); a full base is deleted only when no later increment depends on it, or chains are re-based. Retention changes trigger a sweep and the storage report updates when deletion completes.
  • Honesty: periods with an oplog gap are shown as not restorable to the second; the nearest restorable points are offered.

Competing designs to accept. Logical dumps for small clusters; continuous replication to a standby that is snapshotted; restoring only to snapshot times for cheap tiers; capture from primaries with care for load.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Capture falling behind the oplog window; long replay times; inconsistent cross-shard restore points; corrupted increments; retention not reclaiming storage; drills that only count documents.

Incident guidance.

  • 25-minute gap from a bulk import: capture fell behind a shard whose oplog filled in 40 minutes. Mark the gap, show the customer the restorable points around it, take a fresh snapshot immediately to restart a continuous range. Prevention: headroom alerting, never throttling capture below the write rate, and enlarging oplogs or raising capture capacity when write bursts are detected.
  • Restore misses the {{rto_hours}}-hour promise: replay of oplog since the last snapshot dominated. Communicate the estimate; for the future, more frequent incrementals during heavy write periods, parallel replay per shard, and a restore-time estimate per cluster monitored against the promise.
  • Transaction split across shards in a drill: shards were stopped at their own wall-clock seconds. Restore to a single cluster time on every shard; add a drill check for cross-shard transactions (both sides present or absent).
  • Bill not falling after retention change: references from a running restore and from incremental chains kept snapshots alive. Show "pending deletion" and why; re-base chains so old bases can go; release references when restores finish. Prevention: storage accounting by reference and a sweep report.

Follow-up guidance. Push on the restore-time arithmetic, gap detection, and the cluster-time restore point. Ask what verification proves beyond counts.

Rubric anchors. 2: "daily snapshots plus keep the oplog", no consistency across shards or gap handling. 3: snapshots with cluster-time metadata, continuous capture with gap detection, replay to a point, verification and retention. 4: also restore-time budgeting against {{rto_hours}} hours, cross-shard transaction integrity, reference-counted retention with incremental chains, automated drills with measured durations, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Treats the oplog window as a deadline for capture; defines "to a second" explicitly. Red flags. Wall-clock restore points per shard; no drills; claiming every second is restorable without gap detection.

MDB-L5-01.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • First days: confirm and quantify: pull a sample of the raw records behind the headline number ({{case}}) and classify them; recompute the last quarters with the gamed cases counted honestly (reopened tickets joined to their originals, alerts evaluated at the original thresholds, accepted suggestions checked for later index use). Know how much of the improvement is real before saying anything.
  • Own their part: they reported the number for two quarters without looking underneath; they say so to their manager and to the team.
  • With the team: start privately with the two who built the metric, as a conversation about what the number now rewards, not about who did what; then the whole team, framed as "the target taught us the wrong thing". Invite the team to design the replacement.
  • Replacement: a small set of measures that pull against each other and tie to customer outcomes, such as repeat escalations within 30 days, time to a confirmed fix (customer-verified or measured latency improvement), alert precision (share of alerts that led to action), and index suggestions measured by later use and latency change. Keep a regular review of raw cases (a handful each week), and say how each new measure could be gamed and what would catch it.
  • Upward: tell the manager and the director before the next report, with the corrected history, the reason, and the new measures, so the coming drop is expected and understood.
  • People: for engineers whose goals or promotion cases cite the old number, make sure their real contribution is described in outcome terms and that they are not penalised for doing what the target rewarded.
  • Real example: a metric that drifted from its purpose, how they noticed, what they changed, and the outcome.

Red flags. Naming and shaming individuals; quietly changing the definition so the trend still looks good; replacing one gameable number with another without any cross-check; hiding the corrected history from leadership; a real example where the candidate only noticed and did nothing.

Rubric anchors. 2: "change the metric" without quantifying, owning or communicating. 3: quantifies the real improvement, raises it without blame, replaces with balanced outcome measures, informs leadership early. 4: also owns their own part, protects people whose goals relied on the old number, builds in review of raw cases and anticipates gaming of the new measures, and gives a credible real example with lessons.

MDB-L5-02.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • Check the case, once: a short written summary of their argument and the evidence, shared with the manager to confirm it was understood, plus anything genuinely new (data, a customer case). Ask what the manager is weighing that they cannot see. Not a campaign to reverse the decision.
  • Judgement call versus must-escalate: this is a judgement about risk and value inside the manager's authority, so they commit. They say what would be different (data loss for customers, a legal or safety issue, misleading customers), in which case they would escalate openly, telling the manager first.
  • To the two engineers: honest and loyal at once: "I argued for a different option; the decision was made with reasons I understand; here is how we make it succeed and how we will watch the risk." No hinting that the decision is foolish.
  • Executing well: plan the work properly; reduce the risk they raised through how it is carried out: for weekly restore drills, targeting daily drills at the highest-risk tiers or the most recently changed backup paths; for the schema-migration tool, staged rollout with abort criteria and monitoring of failure rates; for the profiling deprecation, a migration path and direct outreach to the heaviest users. Agree with the manager, in advance, the measure and threshold that would reopen the decision.
  • Evidence either way: report early data whether it supports them or not, and update their own view when it shows they were wrong.
  • Real example: a decision they opposed and carried out, what they did, how it turned out against their prediction, and what they learned about their own judgement.

Red flags. Relitigating repeatedly; complying while signalling to the team that the decision is wrong; slow-walking the work; escalating behind the manager's back; "I just do what I'm told"; a real example where the candidate turned out right and the lesson is only that.

Rubric anchors. 2: either reopens the decision repeatedly or complies silently with no risk management. 3: checks the case was understood, commits, communicates honestly to the team, executes with the risk monitored. 4: also a clear line between judgement calls and must-escalate issues, an agreed trigger to revisit, reporting evidence both ways, and a credible real example with self-aware lessons.

MDB-L5-03.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • Diagnose before drawing boxes: list the systems in {{areas}}, the last two quarters' changes (which code changed together), incidents and customer escalations, and who was involved in each. The symptom ({{symptom}}) is evidence of coordination cost; confirm it with data (meeting load, cross-area reviews, on-call breadth).
  • Boundaries: cut where changes rarely need two teams, often by lifecycle or component (for example backup and restore versus replication and upgrades). Test candidate boundaries against past work: count how many past projects and incidents would have crossed the boundary, and prefer the cut with the fewest. Name tightly coupled systems and give them a single owner with clear contribution rules for the other teams.
  • Ownership transfer: every system, runbook, dashboard, alert and customer escalation path has exactly one owning team, written down. The unloved, frequently paging component gets an owner and an explicit investment (reduce paging, pair the single expert with two others, document).
  • On-call: a transition period with shadow rotations, overlap and named escalation contacts, so no system is thinly covered; on-call breadth per person should fall.
  • People: ask preferences, explain the criteria, place for balance of seniority and skills; choose leads on demonstrated leadership with the manager; for the person not chosen, a real conversation and a concrete growth path.
  • Communication: reasons first, then the proposal, then time for questions; announce to partner teams who to contact for what.
  • Success measures set in advance: cross-team dependencies per project, lead time, on-call pages per person, onboarding time for new engineers, decision participation, retention; a review at three and six months with willingness to adjust.
  • Real example: an organisational change they led or shaped, with what they personally did and what happened.

Red flags. Splitting by headcount or seniority without looking at the work; leaving shared or unloved systems with no owner; switching on-call overnight; a reorganisation announced without reasons; no way to tell whether it worked.

Rubric anchors. 2: "split into two teams of seven" with no boundary reasoning. 3: evidence-based boundaries tested on past work, single ownership, an on-call transition, fair placement and clear communication. 4: also explicit handling of the coupled and unloved systems and the single expert, success measures defined in advance with a review, and a credible real example with lessons.

MDB-L5-04.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • First day: facts to account teams and leadership quickly: the date is missed, the honest cause ({{cause}}), what customers can do now, and when the next update comes. Own the miss, including that warning signs were seen a month earlier and not raised outside the team.
  • New date: give a range with its dependencies and a stated confidence, not a single hopeful date; publish only when the remaining unknowns are understood (for data-loss bugs, after the fix is proven under failover testing). Update on a known schedule even when nothing changed.
  • Customers: direct conversations with the customers who planned around the date, with account teams; workarounds; a limited preview only if the safety evidence supports it, with clear terms; never ship a known data-loss risk to hit a date.
  • Practice changes: estimates with explicit confidence and the assumptions they rest on; a rule that a date risk is raised outside the team as soon as confidence drops below an agreed level; dependency tracking with escalation triggers; a public date only after design is understood.
  • Rebuilding trust: a run of smaller commitments kept and visibly reported; a retrospective shared with stakeholders; no padding of everything, which only moves the problem.
  • Real example: a missed commitment others relied on, how they communicated, what they changed, and how long it took for trust to return.

Red flags. Blaming the dependency team or product leadership; a new date given to soothe people; shipping something unsafe to recover face; silence until the new date is certain; a real example with no personal accountability.

Rubric anchors. 2: apologises and picks a new date. 3: owns the miss, communicates quickly and honestly, gives a range with dependencies, supports affected customers, changes how risks are raised. 4: also explicit handling of the month of unraised warning signs, safety-first reasoning on a preview, trust rebuilt through kept small commitments, and a credible real example with lessons.

MDB-L5-05.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • Overview: a clear problem statement, who depended on the system, real numbers (data size, operations per second, peak to average, latency or freshness targets, cost), the architecture at the right altitude, and the candidate's role.
  • Depth on the chosen angle: for the data model, the entities, their access patterns and keys, and how schema changes were handled; for the hardest failure, the symptom, diagnosis path, root cause, fix and prevention; for the decision to undo, the original reasoning, what was missed, and the cost of undoing it.
  • As a replicated, sharded document database at {{scale}} with {{requirement}}: starts from access patterns: what is read together (embed), what grows without bound or is shared (reference), and what key spreads writes evenly. For records whose shape varies and changes: a schema-version field, validation rules on required fields, migrate-on-read or backfill, and indexes on the common fields. For surviving a region: majority write concern with members placed so no region holds a majority of votes, and an honest latency cost. For outgrowing one machine: a shard key with high cardinality and even write distribution, chosen from the real queries so most are targeted to one shard, with a view on hot customers. For replica reads that never go backwards: causally consistent sessions or primary reads, and why reading any secondary does not give that. Accept other sound answers that fit their system.
  • Honesty: what failed, what they would change, what was the team's versus theirs.

How to judge. Probe numbers (per day or total? peak?), alternatives considered, and one failure in detail. A candidate who owned part of a system and says so precisely scores well; one who claims the whole system but cannot explain its keys, access patterns or failure modes does not.

Red flags. Only buzzwords; numbers that change under questioning; no failure ever; cannot say what they personally did; a document-database answer that embeds everything, ignores unbounded growth, or assumes reads from any replica are always current.

Rubric anchors. 2: high-level description, vague numbers, no clear personal contribution. 3: clear framing with numbers, real depth on the chosen angle, honest failure story, access-pattern-driven document design. 4: also alternatives with evidence, an incremental and correct path to {{requirement}} with its costs stated, crisp separation of own and team contributions, and lessons that show changed practice.
